claims.text: The coating's enhanced creep resistance is caused by its dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructure.
FCC/BCC interfaces act as dislocation-pinning sites.
Pinning at FCC/BCC interfaces impedes dislocation glide under sustained load.
Pinning at FCC/BCC interfaces impedes dislocation climb under sustained load.
The starting protective coating contains both FCC and BCC phases.
The starting coating has a heterogeneous microstructure with distinct FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
The relevant FCC/BCC interfaces are incoherent or semi-coherent.
Incoherent or semi-coherent FCC/BCC interfaces create local stress fields.
The local stress fields at FCC/BCC interfaces are effective barriers to dislocation motion.
Lattice-structure mismatch at FCC/BCC interfaces generates localized back stresses.
Interface-generated back stresses reduce the rate of accumulated plastic deformation under sustained stress.
Under identical loading conditions, the dual-phase coating will have a lower steady-state creep rate than the single-phase control.
Under identical loading conditions, the dual-phase coating will accumulate strain more slowly than the single-phase control.
A single-phase high-entropy-alloy coating lacking significant FCC/BCC boundaries typically has a higher creep rate because dislocation motion is less impeded.
The proposed interface-pinning mechanism remains effective within the coating's operational temperature and stress ranges.
At sufficiently high temperatures or extreme stresses, diffusion creep or grain-boundary sliding may dominate deformation.
Dominance of diffusion creep or grain-boundary sliding diminishes the creep-resistance contribution of FCC/BCC interface pinning.
The contribution of interface spacing and coherency to creep resistance may vary with temperature and stress.
